newsitem.title: RUSSIA: NASA defends decision to swap woman astronaut.
newsitem.headline: NASA defends decision to swap woman astronaut.

text.p: A senior NASA official on Thursday defended the agency's abrupt decision to change astronauts for the next crew to work aboard the Mir space station, dumping a woman who had trained more than a year for the job.
"This has obviously been a very difficult decision," said Frank Culbertson, who heads NASA's joint missions with Russia.

At a news conference at Russian Mission Control, he said problems aboard Mir, which collided with its cargo resupply ship on June 25 and now runs on partial power, made it wise to send someone able to go on spacewalks needed to perform repairs.

He said Wendy Lawrence, who on Wednesday appeared eager to make the journey at a news conference hours before the announcement, was too small for the Russian Orlan space suit and had no spacewalk training, unlike her replacement, David Wolf.
"She was not qualified to operate in the Orlan suit just because of size, and the other alternative of course was to evaluate the back up, David Wolf," Culbertson said.
Lawrence, who is 1.60 metres (five feet, three inches) tall, will still fly on board the U.S. shuttle in mid-September. "She took it very calmly and professionally," he said.
The astronaut swap, which Culbertson apparently first discussed with his Russian counterpart Valery Ryumin on Monday, took many Russian space officials by surprise.
"For us it was very unexpected," said Valery Lyndin, a spokesman for Mission Control outside Moscow.
"There were no objections to her from our side," he said. "We are only sorry she cannot fly, especially since she was so geared up to do such work."
Boris Kryuchkov, deputy director of Russia's Star City cosmonaut training centre, said late on Thursday he had not received any information on a change of crew.
"Yes, we are working with them (the astronauts), but we have not received any such decision yet," he told Reuters. "We have no official documents, decisions, nothing has been decided."

The next Russian crew aboard the 11-year-old Mir will attempt to make vital repairs to the space station, including regaining partial power from the damaged Spektr module by reattaching cables, a job planned for August 20.

Culbertson said the U.S. astronaut was likely to join the ship even if that repair -- crucial to the future of the Mir which has suffered a series of its worst mishaps in the five weeks -- was not a complete success.
"Unless something unpredictable happens...I believe that we could go ahead with the mission," he said. "Right now I'm optimistic."

After those repairs the Russian cosmonauts plan a September 3 spacewalk to inspect the Spektr's punctured exterior, although the NASA astronaut is not expected to participate. They will then return at a later date to make the repairs.

The two Russian cosmonauts who will perform the repairs, Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov, on Thursday left for the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan ahead of their scheduled August 5 blast off to Mir.
Wolf's need for further spacewalk training is likely to delay his departure with the U.S. space shuttle by about 10 days to September 28, Culbertson said.
Wolf, a medical doctor with a degree in electrical engineering, had been scheduled to join Mir in January, and has already been training for several months at Star City, Kryuchkov said.
